utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Registrar, have the accused brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to the interpreters. I want to be sure that they can hear me. Good afternoon to Prosecution and Defence counsel and to the accused. I know that my colleagues are ready, and we can continue with the direct-examination of Witness J.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness J, you were telling us yesterday about the man known as Papa. You told us how you'd seen him brought from the police station by Jelisic. What was Jelisic doing when he brought him out of the police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was walking down the middle of the street towards the river, towards the Sava. He had a baton in his hand and was beating Papa on his shoulders, telling him to hurry, to move quicker because this was the last time he was seeing his town. They then turned the corner by the craft centre and then a shot could be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can the witness please have the aerial photograph again in front of him? By the "craft centre," would you point out what you mean, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's the same small road or lane that you'd seen Jelisic go to on an earlier occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As he went down that lane, what did he do to Papa, or as he reached that lane, what did he do to Papa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said he was dealing him blows with this baton on the back and telling him to go faster, faster. Since the other one's leg had been injured by blows, of course he was moving slowly. He said to him, "Faster, faster."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then you said you heard a shot. I overlooked the fact that you had already told us that. Did you actually see the shooting or did you just hear it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see the shooting or did you just hear it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only heard the shot because they turned the corner into that lane. I could not see it. I was here at that moment, somewhere near that tree [indicates], so I could only hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me turn now to the man Suad. What did you see of what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were then here [indicates], in front of the Oslobodenje kiosk, clearing the splintered glass, we were the only two there, and since he had his back on him, Goran called us, said, "You in the blue jacket, come here." We both were wearing blue jackets and I thought he was calling me. So I turned, but then he said, "No, not you," and then cursed my Balija mother. He said, "You'll be the last one, but the other one." So he took him here towards the entrance into the SUP and ordered him to sing Serb songs and look at the flag. He said that he didn't know how to sing Serb songs, and then he ordered a soldier to bring a rifle with a reinforced butt, and hit him on the shoulders and again ordered him to sing. This one began to cry, and then Goran then said that he didn't like men who cried, and ordered him to start, to start off. He evidently sensed what was going to happen, so he begged him to leave him alive because he had a small child at home, but Goran did not heed to that. He took him the same way, round the corner here, in the lane, and we heard the shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have to move some bodies that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, Jelisic had told you that you were, I think, the strong one, had he not? That's why you would be the last one left to be killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said it right at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he ever repeat that about your being the last one to be killed and the reason why you were being kept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, only when he picked out Suad to take him down there. He said again, "Not you. I told you that you would be the last one." He repeated it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us about the bodies you had to move, where from, where to, and insofar as you can, when you moved them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I took away the body of Amir Novalic, Fric. It was in the building, in the SUP building, in front of the reception office. He was lying there, face down. He had a T-shirt. He had been shot in the back of his head and blood was still coming from his mouth and nose. I was told to take him in front of the Radnik cinema. It is between the Posavina Hotel and the library. It was there, and we carried the body through this park here [indicates]. When I saw that Amir's nose and mouth were bleeding, I asked the soldier to turn him so that the blood wouldn't be dripping on the floor, and then he said to me, "Well, let the Turk wash the streets with his blood," a soldier. I don't know who he was. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: ... when that soldier said that to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you honestly, I did not notice him. He must have been around -- I mean, he may have been there but I just did not see him. I didn't notice him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: ... the second body you had to move?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second body was Sead Karagic's body. It was also in the hall, and we took it to the same place where we'd taken Amir. We left it there, and we then were told to go to the third --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before you moved to the third body, with whom did you move that body? Who else helped you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Senad Muranjkic, called Pidza, and Admir Tolkic helped me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did one of them find the job too much to deal with and get substituted by someone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Amir, little Amir, who asked for that when we took the third body, when he saw that Sead had been castrated, and he was sick. It was very hot, so there were very many flies around Sead and he was sick, and he asked to change places with me, not to have to look at what they'd done to Sead. The third body was behind the SUP building near the Dzindzics' house, somewhere here in this corner here [indicates]. You have to go between these two buildings [indicates], that is SUP and this building, that is, the former Agro Bank, and that is where he was lying face down. He was shot with a bullet at the back of his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you took these bodies across the street and across the small park. What did you do with them? Did you load them onto a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: The third, Hasan's body, we immediately loaded onto the refrigerator, that is, belonging to Bimeks in Brcko, because there was a very visible emblem of the Red Cross, a big one covering the whole door. This vehicle took that particular street and we went through the park, and then we loaded Amir Novalic's and Karadzic's bodies here to this refrigerator, and then I saw Sead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before I turn very briefly to the circumstances of your escape, just a few matters of detail on the evidence you've already told us. The mosque in which you were held, was that near to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Across the street from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you were first kept in the mosque, what did the soldiers say they were going to do to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember only one instance. A soldier, I believe he was one of the White Eagles, he had been wounded. He arrived there and he had an arm wound. He asked for a petrol canister and fired five or six bullets into the floor of the mosque and told us to set fire to it. He said, "I'll set you on fire. Do you see what you've done to me? You've wounded me in the arm, and I will do the same as what you did in Foca." Others only interrogated us, where we lived, what party we belonged to, whether we were members of a party, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On that, was there one senior officer who appeared to be in charge at the mosque or possibly of the whole area around the mosque? If so, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know his name really, but he was very handsome, dark-haired. He was a captain; he had three stars.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a serious-minded man, and he had the right to issue orders to all the soldiers around there, at least that is how it seemed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You don't remember his name now. Do you recall that you may have given a name to the investigators when they took the statement from you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never knew that name, not even in the mosque. Somebody may have heard his name and then put that name instead of me, but I just don't know his name. I only know that his superior was Mauzer for that particular area, and I did not see Mauzer personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. When you saw Jelisic, did you see him alone, or was he ever in the company either of men, women, or girls? What about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I saw him, he was in the company of somebody his age, 23, 24, something like that, a fair-haired guy, more or less the same height, but then he disappeared. The next time, he was in the company of girls, quite young, whom I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were there any of the girls whose names you did know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Monika was the only one I knew (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see anything of an injury on Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he personally -- not to me only, to several other people, he showed me an injury here. He said, "Look what --" I don't know somebody did this, and he had a cut along the forearm. Whether on the left or the right one, I really don't remember. It wasn't a deep wound but some blood was oozing, and then he had his arm bandaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dealing with your escape, was there a man called Slobodan Mitric who you saw on the street and whom you were able to speak to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when Goran took Suad Hadzic away, I was left alone here in the street somewhere. Here [indicating], I think I was here in front of the kiosk, perhaps just slightly nearer than that. I was so out of my wits that I never noticed Slobodan Mitric's car pass by me and stop here by the Posavina Hotel. He was talking to a soldier in a camouflage uniform who was in front of the casino. It was where the casino was. So they talked about something, and I noticed his car. I knew he had a Lada or a PZ, I don't know, but (redacted) (redacted). And I asked Goran Vidovic, who was --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to cut you short because the detail of this may not trouble the Chamber, and it's all in your statement. Were you able to contact Slobodan Mitric? Was he able to have you given special treatment, and eventually you were able to move from one camp to another and eventually you were exchanged in September?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Slobodan Mitric came to me, came out of his car, asked me what I was doing there, and he helped me. He helped me. He got a pass for me. I went to the SUP, and Goran went and he took me to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of all the men who had gone on the street-cleaning exercise that day, how many went back to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: That night, I was the only one who went back and entered the barracks alone, and there were my relatives and friends, and even Petar's brother, asking me about the others. So evidently, nobody else had come before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there. You can give the detail of all that to the Defence counsel, if they wish it, or to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm now going to turn to the lists, if I may. Please may he have those lists. May we go into private session for the reasons which the Court is familiar. The public gallery is quite full, I see, and they may need the position explained to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm going to explain this to the public gallery because these are theoretically always open sessions. We are going to move into a private session because the witness is an individual who is being protected. As you may have noticed, his face does not appear on the screen. The list of names that's going to be mentioned now by the Prosecutor to the witness, as regards certain points, might allow the witness's identity to be known because he comes from a small village and, therefore, showing his face might put into question the protective measures that have been given to him. For the time being, a list is going to be read and it will be read in a private session. Please proceed, Mr. Prosecutor. We're moving into private session now. Are we ready? Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are once again in a public session, and we can move to the Defence for the cross-examination. Mr. Greaves -- let's see. How long did the direct-examination last, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: One hour and five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Is that about how long you're going to need for your cross-examination, Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I would anticipate so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We will apply that time slot with flexibility, which is what the Judges do. All right. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. J, can I ask you please to help us about this: The Prosecution has provided us with two statements that you have made about these matters, one of which you made to the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the date has been -- is unclear when it was that you made it. Can you help us, please, as to which year in which you made it? The only dates that we've got appear to be the 4th of October. Did you make it shortly after you had been released -- I'm sorry, exchanged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should say that I did not give anything by way of a statement to the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They reconstructed the story on the basis of the outline they made, without my knowledge. A neighbour of mine came to see me afterwards. He was chief of a service that was in charge of some kind of security or something in that area, and he came to see me as a neighbour. He was a neighbour. We grew up together. He only asked me what had happened, to describe had happened to him [sic]. He was not alone. There were two men with him, and I saw that there was a young man there taking notes, but afterwards they turned that into a statement and they let me read it. After having read this statement, which actually was not a statement, I saw that there were many inaccurate words that I -- and even names that I did not even mention. When I suggested that this was inaccurate and that it should be done differently, they said, "Well, never mind. This is just an internal matter of our own," and I personally never thought that there would be some kind of a trial or something, so I just let it be. They gave it to me and then I signed it. I said immediately that I did not agree with that statement at all because there are a lot of inaccuracies in there. Also there are some names in there and various expressions like "Serbo-Chetnik." I never used expressions like that. I don't insult people. But they put in certain words that I never said and -- I don't know. They invented some events on the basis my memories.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That's very helpful. I'll come back to that in a moment if I may, please, Mr. J, but can you tell us approximately when this happened in relation to when you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it happened very soon after I was exchanged. Possibly it was in October, because I was exchanged on the 8th of September. I was in Tuzla for some time because my wife and my parents were there, and I brought them closer. Then they heard that I was in this territory and then they came to see me. That's when I just told my story. I did not make a statement. On the basis of this story of mine, they wrote this statement with which I disagree in many points.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So let me just clarify this. You were visited on two occasions by some people. Do you know whom they represented? Did they represent an official body of any kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a security service that had just been set up, because I wasn't really involved in who was doing what at the time, because I was very nervous at the time and I was ill. I had headaches frequently at the time, probably because of the draft in Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: This man approached you and asked you to tell him what had happen. Did he make notes of what you told him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came to my home, this neighbour of mine did, he's a childhood friend, together with two young men whom I did not know. One of those two young men was taking notes. He had some kind of an outline there. Then they probably reconstructed this story which they call a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: On the second occasion you actually read the statement that had been prepared, and although it contained errors, you signed it after their explanation was given to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a war going on. There was shooting all over the place. When I was passing there, there was shooting at the front line and they called out to me. They knocked at the window of their official premises and they asked me to come in. When I said that this was not exactly the way it had happened -- it's not that all of it is untrue, there are quite a few things that are true, but then there are some expressions I never use. They said, "Well, never mind. We just need this for our archives, just so that we'd know what had happened." I signed this very quickly in order to get home as soon as possible. After all, I never saw that statement again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you make it absolutely clear to the people who came to you and asked you to sign it that it contained things which were either inaccurate or untrue? Did you make that absolutely plain to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it loud and clear and they accepted that there probably were some inaccuracies, but then there wasn't enough paper, and there was a war going on, and it can't be retyped. Again, there weren't any typewriters. After all, we had fled from Brcko to that territory. In that way they refused to retype this again and to change anything in this statement. That is what the times were like. I didn't really think about it, that anybody would ever use it for such purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: All right. Mr. J, I'd like just now to ask some quick questions about you personally. In 1995, it's right, isn't it, that you were in the service of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army? Do you still remain in that occupation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the army until 1995, until April 1995. Since then I haven't. I started doing my own work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I don't want to know what you're doing now or anything about your present circumstances, Mr. J. Please understand that. Before the war did you personally take part in political activity, whether as a member of a political party or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not active. I was a member of the SDP, the Social Democratic Party, that grew out of the former communist party. Actively I did not take part in any party because, before the war I was building a house and I didn't feel like going into any kind of politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you remain a member of the SDP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, throughout the war until the present day. Now I'm a bit more active as a social democrat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to turn, please, to your detention at the mosque. Is this correct: that when you were detained and taken to the mosque, you were taken with some 20 to 30 other people? Were you all of them men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And such women and children who had been collected, were they -- I think this is the 4th of May. Were women and children taken to somebody's private residence opposite or near to the mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Across the square from the other mosque, the white mosque, Biljel Dzamija, which is 500 or 600 metres away from the place where they divided us up, because in Brcko there were three mosques in town. This other mosque Bijela Dzamija, the white mosque, was across the street from Dr. Zelenjakovic's house, and since he had a big basement, that's where we put the women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was that used temporarily as a safe place for them to be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was a shelter, because they were shooting in high-rises, and women and children came to that house -- actually, the basement was the safest place, and nobody should have kicked us out of there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I move now please to your arrival at the mosque? Is this right: that there were already other people there when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Again, were they all men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Concerning the group with whom you were brought and that group, were they men between the ages of 18 and 60?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Subsequently, is it right that further people, further men, again also between the ages of 18 and 60, were brought to the mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did that end up with about 200 people being detained at the mosque by the time that night came around?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately about 200. I wasn't counting. There were so many of us that we couldn't move our hands at a given moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I understand that and thank you for the approximate figure, Mr. J. The women and children who had been taken to the private residence, were they subsequently taken to the army barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And subsequently were they also transferred to some other location outside Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: My family was taken to Bjeljina where they spent a few hours, and then they were returned to Brezovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to ask you please if you can help us about this: As far as interrogations which were conducted at the mosque, were those conducted by the soldiers who were guarding you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: The man who was in charge of interrogations was a good looking policeman. He was probably an inspector in the Bjeljina SUP, and he was really in charge of the interrogations. From time to time we were questioned by soldiers too, but that was informal. Officially we were interrogated by a policeman, actually, an inspector in a police uniform, from Bjeljina. That's the way he introduced himself at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. J, that during the course of the interrogations, the questions were obviously personal details, but also as to individual people's political -- party political affiliation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: For example, such as yourself, a member of the former Communist Party, later the Social Democratic Party, were there people who were members of the various political parties, the SDA, and the SDP, and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that those who admitted to being members of the SDA were singled out and were taken and beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: They thought that they would be saved because -- if they would say that he were in the SDA, because they were in power in Brcko because there was a coalition between the SDA and the SDS. They thought that it would be an advantage to be a member of the SDA. At least that's the way it should have been, because they were in a coalition with the SDS, and that is how they were fully in control of the government in Brcko before the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I understand all that, but can you help us, please? Regardless of what the background was, is it right that those who acknowledged being members of the SDA were singled out for beatings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'd like you to help us explain something which you told the Office of the Prosecutor -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. J, I want to ask you about a phrase which you have used in the statement that you made to the Office of the Prosecutor so that you can explain what it means to us, please. In connection with the interrogations of prisoners, you say this: "The suspicious prisoners were taken from the mosque and interrogated in another location." Can you help us, please, as to what you mean by the "suspicious prisoners"? Do you mean by that, people suspected of some crime or some activity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have any time to commit a crime. The crime was belonging to the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. I think, and I won't deal with them again during the course of going through the list of people that you were asked about, but you spoke at one stage during that list about the Terzic cousins or Terzic brothers. Were you aware of them being at the mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. (redacted),

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted). They were together in the mosque, and I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this correct: that they were accused of having weapons and ammunition, but they were returned to the mosque after being interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: The weapons they had were a two-barrelled hunting gun and a hunting sniper, and naturally, they had valid permits issued by the authorities for having hunting weapons and also a certain amount of ammunition that is used for these hunting weapons. Those are all the weapons they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In addition to that, did you, in fact, see someone being beaten in the mosque who had been accused of being a sniper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: A sniper? We were all suspected. Even I was suspected of being a sniper because I went out in slippers, and they said that all snipers had slippers, and of course I wore slippers because I was taken out of my home. One man was beaten up because they found a radio transmitter on him, and this man was a radio amateur and it was only natural that he would have a transmitter at home, and he used it in order to establish contact with other radio amateurs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. J, can I just ask you this: Would this be a fair description of the attitude of those who were detaining you, interrogating you, and suspecting you of being a sniper: that there was in the atmosphere at the time a very high degree of paranoia and fear, whether justified or not, about the activities of people who had been detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'll put it again to you, Mr. J. As far as the people who were detaining you were concerned and the ones who were responsible for interrogating you and other prisoners, is this right: that amongst those people, there was an atmosphere of hysteria and paranoia about snipers and so forth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this young man, who I said was from Bijeljina, he was fair. You could see that he was intelligent, and he carefully selected men who were a bit more useful to him by way of giving information; whereas the others were very haughty, and they wanted to learn things from other people in other ways as to who belonged to a party or whatever. But this man from Bijeljina, he was not paranoid. He was a fair person and he was a calm person.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Does that apply to everybody or is it the case that others were not as calm as this man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said it. He was the only one who was calm. Others brimmed with hatred as they came to see us, as if we'd committed the worst of crimes, even though we were the victims, and yet they posed as if they were the victims and had suffered something, even though we were their detainees whom they had dragged out of our own homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I just ask you briefly about your stay at the army barracks? Did you know the name of the commander at those barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you tell us who it was, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pavle Milinkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Next can I turn, please, to the time when you were at the SUP building? Is this correct: that when you were there, there was a short period outside the building when you were interrogated by a police officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this also right: that the subject of that interrogation was, as far as you were concerned, who you had voted for and your party membership before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And were you also questioned about the SDA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't, only about ZNGs, Young Muslims, what party I belonged to, those sort of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: ZNGs, I think that is not an organisation we've heard about in this case. Can you just explain to us who the ZNGs were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were Croatian units. It was called Narodna Garda, that is, National Guards, and they were active in Croatia. Presumably, they thought they were also active in our area, but I had no knowledge of that, and I don't think they were. There may have been some small groups but not as an organised army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When you were taken inside the building and before, as it were, the commotion started, had you been requestioned by some soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I entered the SUP building, they took us into the hallway. We were going in one line and we were following one another, and I was the first one, it just happened so, so I was sent to the last room as you enter the hall. They put me between two tables and told me to tell them again what I already said outside. One of them even put his automatic rifle next to me, presumably trying to tempt me to try to grab it or something. But that interrogation was very short, not more than a minute or two, because immediately after that, we heard gunfire outside. At that time, I didn't know where it was coming from and what it was due to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So that it's clear, you were asked to go over the subjects you'd already been asked about outside, about which you've just told us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, even outside, I said nothing to Goran. I said again that I knew nothing, that I was a member of the Social Democratic Party. About 500 or 600 metres away from the place where they interrogated me, there was an SDP office, and there he could ascertain that my card was there and that I signed my application for membership that April, April 1992, for the SDP. These archives are in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you just help us about one detail, please, concerning the man Amir Novalic? I think he had a nickname. Can you tell us what that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fric. He was fair-haired. He had fair hair, so this was an association with the Germans, and that's why they called him Fric.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is it within your knowledge that he had been not just a member of the SDA but had been active within the SDA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard that he was a member, but I did not really pay much attention to that because I was not interested in the SDA, and I didn't want to know how active somebody was in any other party. All I was interested in was what people did in my party, in the SDP.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. J, I want to turn now, please, to your brief detention at Luka facility. Is this right: that that was on the 8th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And you were transferred there from the cinema hall at the barracks. Can you tell us at what time that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it was around noon sometime.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How long in all did you spend at the Luka facility before you were released from there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could have been an hour or so. I didn't have a watch with me, nor did I think about time much. I wasn't really interested in time, there was general confusion and fear, but it could have been around one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: To describe what you saw at Luka, would this phrase be right: "utter chaos"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: People were being brought into the camp; people were being released.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, straightaway. They were brought in by buses. There were some local Serb policemen who recognised their friends and their neighbours or even relatives, because there were quite a number of mixed marriages in Brcko, so these people were issued passes straightaway to go back home, and others were kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just help me about this, please, Mr. J: Were you kept outside the buildings at the facility or were you placed inside a building during your period at the camp, at Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You understand what I mean by the phrase "the hangars" as being the storage depots at Luka? Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sure, but I was outside, in front.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. J. I just want to establish precisely where you were. There were, opposite the hangars, a series of administration offices. Were you outside the hangars between those two sets of buildings and the roadway?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And were you able to see all the people who were coming and going, passing and repassing that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You've described people being brought in in buses. Was that the only way in which people were being brought in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that because I was there only a short time, and Slobodan came immediately, saw me there, and took me back to the barracks. How they arrived later, I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I understand that. I was asking only about the period you were there. In terms of numbers, Mr. J, are you able to estimate how many people you saw, as it were, at the camp, detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there could have been over 200, 300, or thereabouts. That would be the number of people I saw there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And of those people, could you give us an estimate, please, of what percentage, what proportion were released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some 10 per cent or thereabouts, but I deduced that from things that happened later. Because at that particular moment, of course, I could not see anything because I was there only a short time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want just to return, very briefly, to the -- and I call it a statement for the sake of convenience -- the account you gave and signed to the Bosnia-Herzegovina Security Authority, Mr. J. Would you accept that in that account, which you signed, you did not make any mention of Goran Jelisic making people sing Serbian songs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time, perhaps the one who was taking those notes down did not think it interesting and simply failed to note it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I understand that. Nor did you make mention there of the name "Adolf" or of the man Adolf saying that you would be the last one to be killed or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only give you the same answer as before, that that fellow could not remember all that I was telling him. I already told you that I wasn't giving a statement. I just gave him some outlines, and he was writing down my account. Of course, he couldn't memorise all that I'd said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'd like to turn, please, with you, Mr. J, in a little more detail, to the lists of people which you were asked to go through and see if you can assist us with any more information about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Perhaps we can go into private session, as is the usual way. I'm sorry. There's one matter before we go into private session. I do apologise. I'm sorry, Your Honour. It's my fault. I missed the note on the other page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. J, I just want to ask you one final thing about Luka and your release. Were you issued with a pass?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody wrote it for me. It was Slobodan who did it on my behalf. I never even saw that pass. He just took it, put it in the glove compartment of his car, and came to fetch me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Subsequently, were you given the pass out of the glove compartment, or were you never given it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never saw it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So although it was issued, it never physically came into your possession?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not need it because I was not released. I was again detained in the barracks, and it only served for going from Luka to the barracks, and then it was not valid any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just briefly, one last question about the passes. Do you know who were issuing the passes at Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said it. Mitric did all that had to be done for me, for my sake. I heard that it was Jelisic who was signing them, but I only heard that. I never saw a single pass. Whether that was true or not, I simply do not know because I just have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume the hearing. Please be seated. Have the accused brought in, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can continue. I hope that all of the interpreters are ready and have rested a little bit. Fine. Very well. Witness J, this is almost the end of this testimony. If you agree, perhaps now the Prosecutor who is going to conduct the re-examination, perhaps Mr. Nice has a few things he'd like to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two very short topics. The first one should probably be in private session. It's about a name on the list.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we want to be in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You've been asked about political parties. You said you were a member of the Social Democratic Party, and it was suggested that there was another party called the SDA. Is it right that you were a member of a party different from the SDA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was your party of single ethnicity or of multi-ethnicity in its composition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Multi-ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What about the SDA? Was there any ethnic limitation on that party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: It defined itself as a party of citizens, but as far as I know, it is uni-national.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Composed of what ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims, Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So whenever someone was identified as of the SDA, was the person being identified Muslim or Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That concludes my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Witness J, the Judges have a few questions to ask you. Let me give the floor immediately to Judge Riad. Judge Riad, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness J. I just have a few clarifications to get from you, if you can. I gathered, especially from your answer to the Defence counsel, that members of the SDA were particularly selected for beating, torture, and eventually killing. Was this exclusive to them? Were they the only people who would undergo this procedure, this beating and torture, or was it a general procedure, and towards whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, it was a general procedure, regardless of party affiliation. Naturally, members of the SDA party were singled out, to a greater extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And why? Was it because they were important, they had a social status in the community, they were leaders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was considered, or they probably considered that members of the SDA party influenced the people in order to vote for secession from the former Yugoslavia, for their independence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Were there other people selected for this beating, that were chosen first among the community? Was there a selection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Who was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most probably, local Serbs, persons who lived in Brcko gave certain qualifications to the persons who did that; that is to say, who were in charge of beatings. They received information from the local Serbs that such and such a person is, for example, a prominent SDA member or held some important post or something, and then that person would be the first to be beaten up or killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did this apply to religious leaders too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In general, was there a religious discrimination? Was it only focused on Muslims, or Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were far less Croats in Brcko anyway. They were beaten up too, but there were less of them because, in the structure of the population, they figured less prominently; therefore, less Croats were beaten up than the Muslims because the Muslims were the majority population in the town of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What about those who were not Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were not on the side of the SDS or in favour of their policy of ethnic cleansing, then they were treated the same way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Even if they were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that certain people, you gave us names, were released from detention and then killed at their home. What was the purpose of this procedure, to release someone and then kill him? Were they killed by other people, by the mob, or were they killed by the same people who took them to gaol, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were different people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Who they are, you don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, it was a group around that Kosta from Modrane, I don't know his last name, the one who came to the mosque and to the barracks. That is from what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And that group was military, paramilitary? What was this group?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is sorry, but we couldn't hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Can you repeat the answer? What was that group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were groups or -- say, a man organises his military group, picks out 100 extremists or so, such as the White Eagles, for instance, the Wolves, and the like of that. They were paramilitaries. They did not belong to any regular army. There was no regular army because the JNA was not a regular army anymore. Yugoslavia had fallen apart at that time; Bosnia-Herzegovina was independent. All the other troops which appeared there were not regular troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was there something which united all these divisions? Was it complete chaos or was there some kind of organisation between them, one purpose, a coordination towards one purpose?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: The groups came to Brcko to provoke chaos. They did have a common leader somewhere above who was not in Brcko, and in Brcko, they were sent there in order to sow fear, to cause panic, to cause chaos, to dislocate as many people as possible, to kill people. In Brcko, I mean, at first glance, they all looked very disorganised, but they all pursued the same goal, to drive away as many Muslims from Brcko as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was the accused, Jelisic, more or less among the leaders of these groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Jelisic only on the 7th of May. After that, I only heard about him, and he looked -- like from the place where I was, he looked like somebody who had an absolute power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Riad. Judge Rodrigues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Witness J, I have a few question. My first is the following: At that time, that is, during the events in Luka, were the Muslims and Croats adversaries or allies in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither adversaries or allies. They were citizens who had been driven away from their homes and, therefore, had been struck by the same ill-fortune, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My second question is that we have heard about the fact that people who were taken aside and beaten were beaten and put aside because they were members of a political party. We have also heard that the SDA had a unilateral or one ethnic group that made it up. Did they choose people who belonged to -- people who were members of the SDA -- when they chose people who were in the SDA, did that mean that they were choosing Muslims? Is it the same thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was only a motive behind it more if you were a SDA member, but other members -- other people of Muslim ethnicity did not fare better either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My third question: Belonging to a political party was a reason that had been mentioned, and being a sniper was another reason given. Having weapons, even with a permit, was yet another reason mentioned. When faced with all of these reasons, was that a real confirmation of that reason or was it only a virtual reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those, yes, were propounded as the main reasons, but the main objective was to terrorise people, to sow terror, to make people feel unsafe, insecure. Seven years after I was driven away from Brcko, I still have no urge to go back to my native town because of the bad memories. I still haven't gone back to my native town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go back to the mosque. You spoke about the separation of men, women, and children. Were the women and children in another location? Does that mean that being at another location, rather, a location other than the mosque, does that mean that they were safer, that the women and children were safer, or was there yet another reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained it once already. Those people would have been safest at home in their cellars, because the cellar was a separate place under the ground and protected against shells and bullets, as that particular locality was shelled. But when we were driven out, there was street fighting still going on where they were shooting at random just to sow fear among people. That was only a temporary station, because they stayed for a very short time in that house, and it was said, "You're not safe here. Let's go to the barracks." Then after the barracks, an hour or two later, "Let's go to Brezovo Polje because there are women and children," and under the pretext of security they simply took them out, away from the place where they used to live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You also spoke about a captain who was more or less the person who was responsible for the mosque. Did that person say anything to you? Did he make a speech to you explaining the reasons why you were there, or did he not say anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember his speech, which sounded like a school lesson. That's how it sounded to me. He was a member of the JNA. He was a Captain, and he was in a JNA uniform, and all the insignia were JNA insignia, from the flag to the rank insignia. He was very -- his attitude was very correct; that is, did he not abuse us in any way. He did not say anything bad. He said something along the lines of this really shouldn't have happened, but we the Muslims were responsible for Bosnia-Herzegovina separating from Yugoslavia, that it should have stayed together. Something like that. It was a kind of a lecture to somehow make us -- to bring it home to us that we were responsible for things that were going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question: In respect of your description of Luka, you said that in the confusion and chaos there were individuals who were released and who were guarded. Do you know whether there was a criterion for making that separation? How were the people selected to be released or to be kept? Could you say whether there was any type of criterion for choosing those who would be released and those who would be kept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose it was when Goran was not somewhere around. So if a neighbour knew you well; or was a friend; or if your best man was a Serb; for instance, my best man was a Serb; then we simply single him out and quickly issue him with a pass and do that. If Goran was there, then presumably on the basis of some references given by people who used to work for the SUP before and who perhaps said, "Well, listen, let this one go, he's quite all right," or something like that, but very few people were released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was there any type of list which listed the names of the people who were to be killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about those lists, but I never saw them, nor do I know anything more about that. I've only heard that there were lists on the basis of which one could know exactly who was to be killed and who was not to be killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the request of Mr. Greaves, you calculated that the percentage of those people who had been released was about ten per cent. Did you hear anything about a percentage that was acceptable to indicate the number of Muslims who were to be kept there, to remain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was detained in the barracks, a friend of mine, that is, a pre-war friend, a Serb, he was a member of some troops, I don't know which, and we talked while I was in the barracks, and he said that they were working on it, working on finding some pass or some permit for me to help me escape, that is, to get across the border of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to go abroad, because he said, "There's no remaining here." The plan was to keep, whether in Bosnia-Herzegovina or Brcko, to only have 20 or 30 per cent of Muslims left here and the rest to deport, to dislocate. That was something that he told me on that occasion, but where did he get that knowledge from, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that "he" planned it. Do you know who planned it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was planned by the one who wanted to bring about -- who wanted to bring about what happened later, that is, the ethnic cleansing of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness J. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not ask you any questions. All of this has been long for you. I see that the Prosecutor is standing, and I should have asked you to sit down, Mr. Nice. Do you have a question or -- All right. The Tribunal asks you very warmly and expresses all of its gratitude to you for showing the courage to come to the Hague, to live again all of these tragic memories which marked your existence during that period. Please do not move. We're going to lower the blinds, and then the Victims and Witnesses Section will take charge of you. We wish you Godspeed back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Mr. Nice or Mr. Tochilovsky would please bring in the next witness. One of you could take him out, then that would have to avoid lowering and raising the blinds constantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before the next witness comes in, there are two little short matters that I should raise, and perhaps they could both be dealt with either in closed session or private session. They relate to the next witness whose summary you should, I think, already have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any summaries here. Judge Riad doesn't, nor does Judge Rodrigues. Oh, yes, now we do. You're talking about Witness K.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed. Witness K, seeks protection of the same type that others have sought, but the first topic I raise relates to her seeking to have present in court a woman whose presence will be of some support and comfort to her, given the particular problems she has faced since the events of which she's going to speak. The account she gives, which is summarised, is an account of incarceration at Luka, where she was repeatedly raped and where she saw the most awful things happening, and that has affected her since to the extent that she has required support in the years that have followed, has benefited from that support and benefits from it still. The group that supports her has sent a representative with her -- oh, it's not private. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness K, thank you for having come. Please remain standing. First, we are going to ask you to identify your name on a piece of paper which is being given to you, but please do not say your name. Simply check to see that that, in fact, is your name. Don't state your name, please. Is that your name? Don't say it; just tell me whether it is. Is that your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are going to take an oath now, which the usher is going to give you. Please read this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Please be seated. Please be seated. Usher, give the witness a glass of water. Try to get a hold of yourself, please, Madam. Take your time. Can we ask the individual who is working with the woman to sit next to her? I think that would be better. Could you please read the oath now? Please. You'll manage. You'll manage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There you are. You were able to do it. Very good. Whenever you need a break, at any point, simply ask us and we will grant the amount of time you need to rest. Please speak calmly. I know you can't be serene; don't even try to be. You are before Judges and you have nothing to fear. Try. If you don't feel good, you have this woman next to you whom you asked to have with you, and you will see that, working together, we'll all get where we need to go. First of all, you're going to be asked questions by the Prosecutor, then by the Defence, and then finally by the Judges. Probably we will not finish this evening, and you will have to come back tomorrow, but that will also give you some time to rest. Mr. Nice, with all the sensitivity that you can show, I know that you are now going to ask the questions that you have to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness K, we call you Witness K in this trial in order to preserve your anonymity. It seems a bit strange but don't worry about that. In fact, you speak pretty good English, but we will have to find out as we go along whether it is going to be better for you to speak in English or to speak in your own language. Some of the Judges don't speak English, so it's all a bit of a muddle here, and we'll just see how we go. To begin with, I'm going to ask you a few questions in English which you can just deal with by yes or no answers, and then we will see where we go from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, all the Judges speak English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that that is the case, but what I was trying to say, rather diffidently, was that sometimes where people from different nationalities are bringing their different English skills together, it is sometimes more difficult to use English and easier to use translation. But I only wish I could -- no, I won't go into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Riad. You see, Witness K, we're saying this in order to try to help you to relax a little bit. Thank you, Judge Riad, and thank you for the kind words that you've said about my English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness K, I think there's been what's called a summary of your evidence prepared, and I think you had a chance to look at it last night; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That summary, which we will get a copy of for you in a minute, was that summary accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know where it is at the moment, but we'll put it before you in a minute. Now, you were trained as a midwife, I think, for several years. How long did it take to become a midwife?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Four years. After that, you worked in the hospital in Brcko as a midwife and had done that for several years. How many years had you been a midwife?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Since 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Here comes the summary. Just have a quick look at this; you don't need to look at it in detail. Is this the summary that you looked at yesterday and that you found to be accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. Thanks very much. Now, having been a midwife for 12 years or thereabouts --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- were you on duty, working at the hospital on the day that the bridges were blown up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. I went at 7.00 morning to work that day, the 1st of May, with my husband, to our duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. You started at 7.00 that morning, the bridges were blown up --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- and then did the next duty of nurses turn up or were there a lot of absentees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Many people were absent from work. They didn't show up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you stay on duty? Because if you hadn't stayed on duty, there would have been nobody to look after the babies.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I could not leave the new babies there. They were fresh.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you stay on duty all night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then was it the next day that all the patients were moved down into the basement of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That hospital, we can look at it on the map if it's necessary, but we've heard of a hospital that is immediately opposite the mosque. Is this hospital immediately opposite a mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Across from the mosque was the community health centre, and then across there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. A little problem is that, as you know, people have to record what we're all saying, and one or two of them are having a tiny bit of difficulty. If you can speak a bit louder, do; otherwise, maybe we can move the microphones a bit closer. See if you can speak up just a touch. What was the date, so far as you can recall it, of the patients all being moved down to the basement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I think the 2nd. It's very hard for me to understand exactly the date, because I was -- I didn't have enough sleep. I was tired.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you think it was the 2nd?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: The 2nd. For that, yeah, but I think the 2nd, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not that important, so don't worry. I think then or on the following day, the 3rd, explosions seemed to be getting louder and closer, and you started to receive wounded people in the hospital who were suffering from firearms injuries; is that right? Just yes or no will do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then you and the remaining medical staff did as well as you could for the people who were coming in and, indeed, for the women and the babies who were already there. I think that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next thing that happened -- if you can estimate the day, do so, but if you can't it doesn't mater. Is it the next thing that happened is that you became aware of Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: The patient was arrived which were wounded. They will tell us, you know, what they saw to the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, but did you actually see Serb soldiers in the hospital at one stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No. Until they come do occupy, the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What is the day that they occupied, the Serbs, roughly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: 3rd or 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did they completely occupy the hospital? We don't need to deal with this in detail, but just tell us, did they completely occupy the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did they have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did they have painted faces, some of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, all of them. All of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you get the name of the soldier who appeared to be in charge of all these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic, because he was working in the hospital as a guardian. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. But what was the name of the Serb soldier, the Serb boss soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: With him, he was -- the name was from the Serbian name, with the accent, Bozo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But the name of the Serb -- what was the name of the chief Serb soldier, if you can remember it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. When they arrived, more soldiers there with the group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was in charge of that group of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Mauzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mauzer. Thank you. Did there come a time when everyone in the hospital, or perhaps most of you, I don't know, were all gathered up and spoken to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: They would send a soldier all around the hospital to let us to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What were you told when you were all gathered up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: We will stay in the cafeteria, in that area, and they will told us, you know, the one who is taking that territory, taking the power, we have to obey them, otherwise, we will be killed. So they will try to ask questions of some of our doctors in the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, they asked questions of the doctors. Did they treat the doctors well or badly at that stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Bad. Badly, badly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did they actually beat them in the hospital or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But taking the story forward, just to get along a bit, were you, along with other people, taken from the hospital to Luka, a place down on the river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: After they finished that lecture, they will send us out on our -- on the work, and after while, like evening-time, I don't know exactly what time, but it was evening, because of the duty, they be giving the therapy, some soldier, they will come and ask for my name, and he will say in the hallway, (redacted) 24 [redacted]."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So he had your name and he was looking for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we now delete that, obviously, from the record, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My mistake to have allowed you to say that, but don't mention your name. It's all right. It won't go out. Don't worry. The staff here can take care of that sort of problem. It's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing to thank us for.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: After that I follow him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Were you taken off to Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: They brought us in the basement, in the hallway. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: (redacted). They told me to stay next to them in the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, to take the story quickly, because we can deal with it quite quickly, this bit, you were put in a van and you were taken to Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As you drove through the town of Luka, did you see the destruction that had already taken place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. It was terrible. It was terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Then when you got to Luka -- we know about what Luka looks like because we've got lots of photographs. So don't worry about that. We know that there are hangars on one side and little low buildings on the other, and we can show you a diagram or your diagram of it if you like, but when you first got there, did you go to the hangars or to the buildings opposite?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: They took us first in the office, and it was, you know, walking around and -- in the yard between the hangar it was, you know, police people walking around.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. What did they say was going to happen to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: They took us inside in the office, and there's a procedure. Just, you know, basic -- just they ask basic question. You know, no need to worry. And even the policeman, he was very polite. He was offer us drink and try to make comfort.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But did you then see another man come into the office, a man whose name you didn't know at the time but you later learnt what his name was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Actually, another person, Ranko is inside the office and disturb, you know, even -- he was in the police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I think you mentioned a name. Was it Ranko? It's not on the screen but it doesn't matter. Did you say the name "Ranko"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: At that time I didn't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But was he the man in the office or was he the man who came into the office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Who is come from outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Actually, he was run to his -- you know, it was quick happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When he came into the office -- again you can deal with this bit very quickly, although, it may be unpleasant -- what did he do to somebody who was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: He throw outside another policeman, and the policeman tried to make him calm down, and then we will stay only with that person who looks like crazy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did he do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: First he was shot in the air with his gun, and then he started cursing the others and yelling very loud, and he just curse us as Muslim. He wants to all kill us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then did he do something to one of the men there, and if so, to which man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. He approached the first, (redacted), threw him on the ground and he hit him with a gun, you know, bottom part, so bad, and with the boots walk over to the head from -- you know, all body --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How was (redacted) --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: -- and hitting with the gun. After that, he took (redacted), another man --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is the house painter -- not the house painter, the -- well, the house painter that you'd come with from the hospital, I think.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did he do to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: He will do the same, throw him the ground, and the same tactic, you know, beat him with a gun, with the boots, kicking and walking.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that the other house painter that had come with you from the hospital or was that someone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Actually, that's first (redacted) and then first the house painter, (redacted) [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then what did he make those men do to each other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: (redacted). He will order to them get up on the feet. Then he was so tired and frustrated from the beating, look exhaust, and then he will order to us beat each other like boxing, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the doctor, and the house painters, and yourself, were you compelled to try and do what you wanted to do, to beat each other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, only I didn't hit. You know, probably I -- they feel I'm weak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, when that was over, were you taken outside or told to go outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. With the gun he took us so fast, pushing us to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I ask the witness to have a look at this exhibit? It's amended to the extent of the name being taken out and replaced by "Witness K" at the top, if I can hand it in. There is an original which can be provided, under seal, which has the name on it. It's a matter for the Court whether the original need go in. While that's being circulated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
